chunks: "A chip needs multiple clock domains because different parts have different needs, and forcing everything onto one clock would cost power, area and performance.
First, required speeds differ. A CPU core may run at 2 to 4 gigahertz, but a UART or I2C block only needs a few MHz, and the always-on timer runs from a 32 kilohertz crystal.
Running everything at CPU speed would burn dynamic power, alpha C V squared f , for no benefit.
Second, many interfaces have clocks set by standards or external devices: USB, Ethernet, PCIe, DDR, a camera or display.
The chip has to sample or generate data at whatever rate those protocols define, so those blocks get their own clock, often from their own PLL.
Third, power management: with separate domains I can scale the voltage and frequency of the GPU independently of the CPU, or gate the clock of an idle block entirely.
Fourth, physical design: distributing one gigahertz clock with low skew across a large die is expensive, so splitting into smaller domains keeps clock trees tractable.
The cost is crossing between domains. A signal launched by one clock and captured by an unrelated clock can violate setup or hold and make the flop metastable.
So I use synchronizers, usually two flip-flops in series for single bits, and for buses I use a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers so only one bit changes at a time.
CDC checks are part of sign-off."
